transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you so much for fitting me in. I, um... I hope I'm not taking up too much of your time. 

I'm really just here because... well, I want to make sure I'm doing the right thing, and I guess I just need someone to talk to about what's been going on. For months now, I’ve been seeing this same pattern, and I really don't want to sound difficult—I supervise an office, so I always try to be very reasonable and easy to work with—but... my sister’s appointments keep getting moved around without anyone telling me, and her bills keep showing up with all these little errors on them. And the people involved just constantly 'forget' to call me back. 

Everyone keeps telling me I'm overreacting and that they're just honest mistakes. And I know people make mistakes, I really do, but... I just know they’re keeping information from me. It really feels like they are actively trying to push me out of making any decisions. 

I'm sorry, does that make sense? I hope I don't sound silly saying all of that out loud.

Aside from this situation with your sister's care, would you say you generally have a hard time trusting other people in your life—like coworkers, friends, or family—even when there's no clear reason to suspect them?

Oh, goodness, no. No, not at all. I actually... I pride myself on having a really good relationship with my coworkers. My team at the office is just wonderful, and I trust them completely. I really am not a suspicious person by nature, Doctor, I promise. I always try to give people the benefit of the doubt. I mean, you kind of have to in my line of work, right? 

That's part of why this whole situation with my sister's care is so upsetting to me. It's just so unlike me to feel this way. I usually never have any issues trusting my friends or the rest of my family. I just don't want you to think I'm someone who goes around looking for problems, because I'm really, really not. 

Is that... is that helpful to know? I hope I'm answering your questions okay.

If someone showed you clear evidence that these scheduling mix-ups and billing errors were truly accidental, do you think that would change your mind, or would you still feel that people are intentionally trying to keep information from you?

I mean... I really, really wish I could just look at a piece of paper and say, 'Oh, silly me, it was just a typo.' I want to be reasonable, I truly do. But... and I know I already brought this up, so I'm sorry to repeat myself... it’s just been months of this exact same pattern. 

Even if someone showed me something that looked like proof of an accident, I just... I don't think I could ignore what I know is happening. Because when the appointments keep getting moved, and the bills are always wrong, and they just happen to 'forget' to call me back over and over... even when everyone else tells me they are just innocent mistakes, I just know they aren't. I know they are keeping information from me on purpose. They really are trying to push me out of making decisions for her, no matter what kind of excuse they might put on paper. 

I'm not trying to be difficult or stubborn, I promise. I just can't pretend it's not happening when it's so clear to me. Does that make me sound completely unreasonable? I really value your professional opinion on this, and I want to make sure I'm explaining myself properly.
Can you tell me when these suspicions first started—did they begin around the same time as some specific event or change in your sister's health or care situation?

Well, um... yes, actually, that's a very good point. It’s been... gosh, I’d say about 11 months now? It all started right around the time my sister’s health suddenly got worse, and I had to step in to start coordinating her care. 

I was just trying to be a good sister, you know? I wanted to make sure everything was organized and taken care of properly. I really don't want to sound like I'm complaining about having to help her, because I love her dearly and I'm more than happy to do it. It's just that... well, that's exactly when all these issues with the staff and the appointments started happening. 

Does that timeline make sense to you? I hope I'm giving you the right kind of information.

Besides feeling that people are keeping information from you, have you noticed other symptoms since this all began—like trouble sleeping, feeling on edge, or excessive worry that's affected your daily life?

Oh, no, definitely not. I mean... I do worry about my sister, of course, because I care about her, but it hasn't affected my daily life like that at all. Outside of dealing with her appointments and just... trying to get straight answers from that office, everything else is perfectly normal. 

I still keep my home in order, I pay all my bills on time, and I go to work every day and do my job just like always. I know maybe... well, I suppose some people might think I’m a little too focused on this whole situation with her care. But I promise you, I'm not falling apart or acting strangely in any other part of my life. I'm holding it all together very well, just like I always have. 

I hope that reassures you? I just really want you to know that I'm still managing all my responsibilities properly. Did I answer that okay?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a single, well-organized, fixed persecutory delusion (that staff are intentionally withholding information and trying to exclude her from her sister's care decisions) that has persisted for approximately 11 months. The belief is circumscribed to this one situational context—she explicitly denies generalized distrust of coworkers, friends, or family, and denies any broader paranoid traits, ruling out Paranoid Personality Disorder (F60.0). She maintains full occupational and daily functioning (goes to work, manages household, pays bills on time), and denies significant anxiety, sleep disturbance, or mood symptoms, arguing against an Adjustment Disorder with anxiety (F43.23). There is no evidence of hallucinations, disorganized speech/behavior, or negative symptoms, which would suggest a primary psychotic disorder like schizophrenia. The delusion is non-bizarre (plausible scenario of institutional neglect/exclusion), encapsulated, and the patient retains insight into how the belief might appear to others (repeatedly asking if she 'sounds unreasonable'), though she cannot be dissuaded by counter-evidence, meeting criteria for a fixed delusion of the persecutory type. This clinical picture—an isolated, non-bizarre, persistent delusion in the absence of other psychotic or mood symptoms, with preserved functioning outside the delusional theme—is most consistent with Delusional Disorder (F22), persecutory subtype.
